    Cosmic Civilisations · Formulating the Method

    How fast does energy climb?

    Watch energy grow for 2,500 years. The picture goes from a city, to the Earth, to a shell around the Sun at the Earth's distance.

    The numbers follow the path that reaches ten billion times today's energy. That is still only one ten-thousandth of the Sun.

    Lem writes that earthly energy would grow by one third of a percent a year, and that in 2,500 years it would be ten billion times larger, one ten-thousandth of the Sun's output by the year 4500. He gives the Sun as 4×10^33 erg a second, caught by a shell at the Earth's distance.

    One third of a percent a year for 2,500 years multiplies energy by about 4,100, not ten billion. The rate that does reach ten billion times in 2,500 years is about 0.925 percent a year. The picture follows that ten-billion-times path. Lem's sentences stay as he wrote them.

      Cosmic Civilisations · Formulating the Method

      Can we hear them?

      A dish like Earth's can hear an Earth-like transmitter out to about ten light-years. Drag the star farther and the rings fade. To be heard a hundred times farther, the signal must be ten thousand times stronger.

      Tap the speaker to hear a soft ping. The ping stays quieter more gently than the rings, so it does not vanish at once. That loudness is ours.

      Lem says Drake's 1960 receiver, following Cocconi and Morrison, could take signals from about ten light-years, and from a hundred times farther if the signal were strong enough. He describes the antenna as 27 metres.

      The inverse-square law is our physics, not a formula Lem writes down. Power grows with the square of distance. A hundred times farther needs ten thousand times the power. The beacon's loudness uses a decibel curve with a floor, so a far star stays a quiet ping.

      Letter to the stars

      Send a question to a star 1,000 light-years away. The question takes 1,000 years. The reply takes another 1,000. On Earth, about 80 generations pass.

      Technical details

      Project Ozma used an 85-foot dish, about 26 metres. Lem's 27 metres stays as he wrote it.

      Cosmic Civilisations · Statistics of Cosmic Civilisations

      How many civilisations are awake at once?

      Our illustration, not Lem's model.

      Lem reports a picture from Bracewell and von Hoerner: about 150 billion stars, and only one star in 150 with planets, so about a billion planetary systems. A short-lived civilisation leaves few neighbours awake. The lights, the disc and the distances drawn here are our picture. Lem's own spacings stay as separate marks.

        Cosmic Civilisations · A Metatheory of Miracles

        Could a technetium line be an engineered star?

        In this section Lem reports that Shklovsky, half in jest, named two possible feats of astro-engineering: artificial supernovae, or technetium lines in the spectra of some rare stars. Technetium does not linger. Lem says it fades within a few thousand years, so a visible line might mean someone had sprinkled a few million tonnes into the star. He then turns to Ockham’s razor. The drawing is a schematic, not a measured spectrum. The stars named below are later astronomical examples.

              Cosmic Civilisations · Human Uniqueness

              When does a rare throw become likely?

              Lem paraphrases Baumsztejn's argument. He does not quote the calculations. One player throwing ten sixes is extremely unlikely. A billion players at once make that chance far greater. About three million cod eggs in one spawning yield one adult fish, and he calls the chance of at least one or two fish a certainty.

              Our calculation: a billion players give a chance of about 0.9999999343, which in this picture is almost certain. The rolls, the curve, the crowd and the per-egg chance are our illustration, not Lem's model. One egg in three million is our reading of one fish from three million eggs. That reading is not the certainty he names for one or two fish.

              One throw almost never gives ten sixes. But with enough players, someone almost surely does.

              Pick how many people throw. Gold means someone in that group got ten sixes.

              One egg almost never becomes a fish. Pick how many eggs.

              The chance on the readout is our calculation, not the certainty Lem names.

              Lem's clutch is about three million eggs, and he accepts that one adult fish comes from it. He calls the chance of at least one or two fish a certainty. He does not give the chance for a single egg.

              Chance of at least one fish

              Lem's objection: an egg that never becomes a fish is destroyed. A line of animals that never becomes human can still lead to minds another way. Evolution is not a dice game that only wins or loses.

              Technical details

              The chance one player throws ten sixes is 6 to the power −10. The chance at least one of N players does it is one minus the quantity (1 − that chance) to the power N, computed as −expm1(N · log1p(−p)) so a tiny chance does not vanish. The egg chance per egg is one divided by three million, our reading of “one fish from three million eggs”. The rolls use a seeded sequence in Ada, so the same roll number always shows the same faces.

              Intellectronics · Return to Earth

              What does persistent doubling imply?

              A normalised index starts at 1. The doubling time of 15 years follows a historical discussion of scientific periodicals. The year 2026 only places that horizon on a calendar. Ada computes one exponential. It is a scenario, not a forecast.

              N = N₀ · 2^(t / d)

              The factor is 2^(t / d) even when the starting quantity is zero. The quantity is then zero.

              The same exponential applies for the whole horizon. A shorter doubling time is not a tipping point.

              A whole year from -10000 to 10000. 2026 is a presentation choice, not a measured date.

              Illustrative level. The default 10 is not a forecast.

              Intellectronics · Return to Earth

              How many prizes does a lottery return when some tickets are blank?

              A lottery has a fixed pile of tickets. Some tickets win a prize, and the rest are blank. You buy some tickets, and each ticket can be bought only once. The page gives the average number of prizes over many repeats, and the chance that this one purchase wins nothing.

              Small example fills a teaching lottery. It is not a quotation. Book sizes fill one million tickets, one thousand prizes, and buying half of the tickets. Changing a number clears the selected button.

              Expected prizes

              Chance of winning nothing

              Chance of at least one prize

              Expected prizes is the average over many repeats of the same lottery. One draw can win more, or fewer, or nothing.

              Expected prizes

              Expected prizes

              Tickets you buy

                Chance of winning nothing

                Chance of winning nothing

                Tickets you buy

                  The left chart counts prizes. The right chart is a chance from 0 to 1. A point on the zero line is a chance of exactly zero. A smaller positive chance is left off that line; read the number above the chart.

                  Technical and math details

                  Expected prizes = tickets bought × prizes / tickets in the lottery. The chance of winning nothing is the number of ways to choose every bought ticket from the blank tickets, divided by the number of ways to choose from all the tickets. If the bought tickets must include a prize, that chance is exactly zero.

                  This counts the lottery analogy in Return to Earth. It does not show that research directions are chosen uniformly at random, and it is not a prediction of discoveries. The small example is not a quotation. The million tickets, the thousand prizes, and buying half are the sizes named for that analogy.

                  Intellectronics · The Megabit Bomb

                  What happens when the researcher index doubles faster than discoveries?

                  Two indices each start at 1. That starting 1 is our scale, not a census. In the book’s comparison, discoveries double every 30 years and the researcher index doubles every 10. The page follows both curves and divides them. It does not predict that hiring a person creates a discovery.

                  Book times fill the 30-year and 10-year doublings and look 30 years ahead. Same pace sets both doublings to 30 years, so you can see the indices stay in step. Same pace is ours, not a figure from the book. Changing a number clears the selected button.

                  Discovery index

                  Discoveries per researcher index

                  The ratio is the discovery index divided by the researcher index. It is not a count of discoveries each person will make.

                      Phantomology · Teletaxy and Phantomultiplication

                      How long before a reply can return?

                      Teletaxy is action at a distance. A signal here travels at the speed of light in vacuum, over a distance that does not change. The same wait is why an interstellar conversation cannot stay prompt. The presets are familiar examples, not one formula taken from the book.

                      Variable distances use a chosen alignment, not today’s positions. Europa and Titan lie beyond their planets, not at the planet’s distance from the Sun. Proxima Centauri is the nearest star of Alpha Centauri, not the A and B pair.

                      Signal arrives

                      Reply arrives

                      Timeline

                        Sources and exact seconds

                        Vacuum speed of light: 299,792,458 m/s, the SI definition of the metre. Astronomical unit: 149,597,870,700 m exactly, IAU 2012 Resolution B2; the Earth–Sun preset is 1 au. Light-year: one Julian year of 365.25 days of 86,400 s, as recognised by the IAU. Moon: NASA’s stated average, 384,400 km. Venus: NASA fact sheet, mean distance at inferior conjunction, 41.39 million km. Mars: 225 million km, a round figure for the often cited average of about 140 million miles. Europa: NASA’s mean Jupiter opposition, 628.81 million km, plus Europa’s orbital distance 671,000 km on the far side. Titan: difference of the NASA Saturn and Earth semimajor axes, 1,282.443 million km, plus Titan’s orbital distance 1,222,000 km on the far side. Proxima Centauri, Alpha Centauri C: 4.2465 light-years from the Gaia DR3 parallax. None of these is today’s ephemeris.

                        Creating Worlds · Cultivating Information

                        How many yes-or-no answers does it take to say which sequence happened?

                        A bit is one yes-or-no. A coin has 2 outcomes each toss, a die has 6 faces, and this alphabet has 26 letters. Choose how many outcomes are possible each time, and how many times that happens.

                        Each button fills both numbers. The selected button stays marked. Changing a number clears that selection.

                        Information for one turn

                        Information for the whole sequence

                        Possible sequences

                        Information needed

                        Left to right is the number of times. Upwards is the information needed to record the sequence. The line is that information. The dot is the result for the number of times you entered.

                        Information needed (bits)

                        Number of times

                          Technical and math details

                          The count treats every outcome as equally likely, and every turn as independent of the others. It does not measure meaning, knowledge, or how a real file would be compressed.

                          One turn is log2 of the number of outcomes. The whole sequence multiplies that by the number of times. The number of sequences is the outcomes raised to that number of times.

                          Creating Worlds, Cultivating Information, discusses selective information with a logarithmic measure, and contrasts a small set of element statements, about 100, with a vocabulary-sized set. This page does not treat 100 as a quoted exact vocabulary, and it does not quote a coin, a die or an alphabet from the book.

                          The result above can be a fraction of a bit. That is the theoretical amount. A fixed-length code stores a whole number of yes-or-no bits per turn, which can be more. A die is about 2.585 bits in theory and 3 stored bits in that kind of code. Those are different numbers.

                          A Lampoon of Evolution · Constructing Life

                          How much information fits in a given time?

                          Constructing Life sets three unlike historical figures side by side: a low-redundancy printed page of about 10,000 bits, a human mind coping with about 25 bits each second, and a bacterium producing at least 1,000 bits each second. This card divides a quantity by a constant rate, or multiplies that rate by a duration. It does not show that a bacterium reads a page, and 25 bits/s is not a measured brain bandwidth.

                          Lem’s example restores 10,000 bits, 25 bits/s and 400 s, and draws the human and bacterial curves.

                          Information in this duration

                          Linear scales. Information grows in proportion to time. The slope is the rate.

                              Digital link, nominal line rate

                              This is the nominal 1000 Mb/s line rate of IEEE 802.3 1000BASE-T. It is not framed payload, not a measured processing speed, and not machine understanding. The time is an ideal constant rate for the quantity above. When this rate is chosen, the chart compares it with the human figure only.

                              Nominal line rate

                              Time for this quantity at that rate

                              The historical human and bacterial figures are not the same kind of information as each other, or as this line rate. Spike counts, DNA alphabet capacity and task information are not on the chart.

                              Sources and what is not compared

                              The three figures are the historical comparison in Stanisław Lem, Summa Technologiae, Constructing Life.

                              The digital reference is the nominal 1000 Mb/s operation in IEEE Std 802.3 (1000BASE-T, originally IEEE 802.3ab-1999; the GMII in Clause 35 supports only 1000 Mb/s). One megabit is 1,000,000 bits. The time divides the quantity by 1,000,000,000 bits/s and ignores framing, interpacket gaps and encoding, so it is not payload throughput.

                              Technical demonstration

                              Add two numbers

                              These two numbers are already filled in. Change either one and the sum updates. Ada does the addition. This is a boundary test, not a chapter calculator.

                              Result

                              Use a dot as the decimal separator in every language. Ada receives the binary64 value, not translated text.

                              Contract: finite binary64 addition. A negative finite operand is an ordinary value. A non-finite operand or a non-finite sum is an error. Underflow to a finite result, including zero, is success. Tolerance for the published integer fixtures is exact binary64 equality.
